title: Why Conegliano Valdobbiadene tastes the way it does

lede.text: Glera grown on hill country around Conegliano and Valdobbiadene makes still and sparkling wines. One traditional sub-zone, Cartizze, has a mention of its own.

chapters.title: Hill country and a sub-zone
paras: The grapes come from the hill country of a set list of communes, Conegliano among them. The name pairs Prosecco with both towns or with either one alone.
Inside the zone, Cartizze is a traditional sub-zone with its own mention.

fly.label: Cartizze
fly.caption: Cartizze is the traditional sub-zone whose spumante may carry the mention Superiore di Cartizze.

chapters.title: Glera, still and sparkling
paras: Glera is the grape. Up to 15% may come from four other grapes grown on the same farm: Verdiso, Bianchetta trevigiana, Perera and Glera lunga.
The wine can be still. It can be frizzante, which is lightly sparkling. Spumante, which is fully sparkling, always carries the mention superiore.
Spumante can add "sui lieviti" (on its yeasts). It can also add "Rive", followed by a named place from the rules' annex A. "Superiore di Cartizze" is for spumante from the Cartizze sub-zone only.
The area became a DOC in 1969 as Prosecco di Conegliano Valdobbiadene. It became a DOCG in 2009.
